50-001.r: 19th-century religious reform movements → mainly attracted intellectuals, urban upper castes and liberal princes (middle class); poor ordinary classes stayed largely outside.

50-002.r: Both true, R explains A: 19th-century socio-religious movements modernised India because rationalism and scientific temper were at their core.

50-003.r: Educated Hindu middle class → first influenced by Western civilisation (rationalism, scientism, humanism); rejected superstition, pilgrimage and idolatry.

50-004.r: Raja Ram Mohan Roy → 'Father of Indian Renaissance'; also 'Father of Modern India', 'Father of Indian Nationalism', 'First Modern Man', 'Yugadoot'.

50-005.r: Father of Indian Nationalism → Raja Ram Mohan Roy (not Gokhale, Tilak or S.N. Banerjee, so 'None of the above'); also Father of Indian Renaissance, Maker of Modern India.

50-011.r: Ram Mohan Roy's first society → Atmiya Sabha (1815, monotheism); then Brahmo Sabha (1828), later Brahmo Samaj. Tattvabodhini Sabha (1839) → Devendranath Tagore.

50-013.r: Brahmo Samaj → founded by Raja Ram Mohan Roy as Brahmo Sabha on 20 August 1828; rejected idolatry, believed in one God.
50-013.c: No answer printed: the correct year 1828 is not among the options.

50-014.r: Brahmo Samaj → founded by Ram Mohan Roy, 20 August 1828, Calcutta; Debendranath Tagore joined 1843 and appointed Keshab Chandra Sen its chief Acharya.
50-014.t: Founder = Ram Mohan Roy, not Keshab Chandra Sen (who was only made Acharya by Debendranath Tagore).

50-018.r: Mughal emperor Akbar II → gave Ram Mohan Roy the title 'Raja' (1830); Roy died 27 September 1833 at Stapleton near Bristol, where his Samadhi is.

50-021.r: Keshab Chandra Sen → Tabernacle of New Dispensation and Indian Reform Association (29 October 1870). Calcutta Unitarian Committee → Ram Mohan Roy, Dwarkanath Tagore, William Adam.

50-022.r: Keshab Chandra Sen → founded Bhartiya Brahmo Samaj (Brahmo Samaj of India), 11 November 1866, after Devendranath Tagore removed him as Acharya; Tagore's group became Adi Brahmo Samaj.
50-022.t: Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878) → Anand Mohan Bose and Shivnath Shastri, against Sen's under-14 daughter's marriage.

50-023.r: Adi Brahmo Samaj → Devendranath Tagore; Keshab Chandra Sen left after losing the 'Acharya' title and formed Brahmo Samaj of India (1866).
50-023.t: Don't swap: Adi = Devendranath Tagore; Brahmo Samaj of India = Keshab Chandra Sen.

50-024.r: Brahmo Samaj → based on monotheism (one God); opposed idolatry and anthropomorphism; universal worship of God.

50-025.r: Ram Mohan Roy opposed child marriage, Sati and idolatry, but strongly supported Western education through English (letter to Lord Amherst, 11 December 1823).

50-026.r: 'Samachar Chandrika' (1822) → Bhavani Charan Bandyopadhyay, started to oppose Ram Mohan Roy's religious/social ideas; he had earlier edited 'Samvad Kaumudi'.

50-027.r: Both correct: Ram Mohan Roy respected traditional Eastern philosophy and wanted Indians to adopt a rational, scientific approach, human dignity and equality of men and women.

50-028.r: Brahmo Samaj → opposed idolatry and the dominance of priests (1, 2 correct). 'Vedas are infallible' was Dayanand Saraswati's doctrine, not Brahmo Samaj's.
50-028.t: Don't confuse Brahmo Samaj (anti-idolatry, anti-priest) with Dayanand Saraswati (Vedas infallible).

50-029.r: A false, R true: 'Samvad Kaumudi' (4 December 1821) was launched by Ram Mohan Roy but officially edited by Bhavanicharan Bandopadhyay; it campaigned against Sati (widow burning).

50-030.r: Debendranath Tagore → Tattvabodhini Sabha, Kolkata, 1839, to spread Ram Mohan Roy's ideas and the Upanishads; merged into Brahmo Samaj in 1859.

50-031.r: Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902) → best representative of Neo-Hinduism; simplified Ramakrishna's teachings; spoke at Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 1893.

50-033.r: Swami Vivekananda → represented India at the Parliament of the World's Religions, Chicago, 1893; spoke on 'The meaning of the Hindu religion'.
50-033.c: All options (1863, 1892, 1881, 1894) are wrong; MPPSC gave bonus marks.

50-037.r: 'Practical Vedanta' → Swami Vivekananda; Vedanta practised in every sphere of life; first speech on it in London, 10 November 1896.

50-038.r: Swami Vivekananda → wrote Jnana Yoga, Karma Yoga, Raja Yoga and Bhakti Yoga.

50-039.r: Ramakrishna Mission → founded 1897 by Swami Vivekananda in the name of his guru Ramakrishna Paramhamsa; headquarters Belur, Howrah (West Bengal).
50-039.t: Founder = disciple Vivekananda, not Ramakrishna Paramhamsa himself.

50-044.r: Ramakrishna Mission (Association) → founded by Swami Vivekananda in May 1897, with his sanyasi associates and lay disciples of Sri Ramakrishna.

50-045.r: Sharadamani (Sharada Devi) → wife of Ramakrishna Paramhansa (married 1859).

50-046.r: "I have no time to think about God because a lot of work has to be done on this earth" → Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar.

50-047.r: "The British Empire is rotten to the core, corrupt in every direction and tyrannical and mean" → Sister Nivedita.

50-048.r: Swami Dayanand Saraswati → Arya Samaj, April 1875, Bombay (Mumbai); its headquarters set up at Lahore in 1877.

50-051.r: Swami Dayanand Saraswati → revival of the Vedas, slogan 'Go back to the Vedas'; called 'Martin Luther of India'; raised 'Pakhand Khandini Pataka' (1867).

50-054.r: 'Satyarth Prakash' (Light of Truth, 1875) → Swami Dayanand Saraswati; sacred book of Arya Samaj. Dayanand's original name Mool Shankar (born 1824, Morvi, Gujarat).

50-059.r: Shuddhi movement → Arya Samaj; to bring converts back into Hinduism.

50-060.r: Both true, R not the explanation: Arya Samaj gave Hindus self-confidence and self-reliance; it also rejected belief in White Race superiority.

50-062.r: Swami Dayanand → first used the word 'Swaraj', declared Hindi the national language, first urged Swadeshi and boycott of foreign goods.

50-063.r: "India for the Indians" → Dayananda Saraswati (his political message against Western domination).

50-064.r: Chronology: Tulsidas (16th century) → Ram Mohan Roy (1772-1833) → Dayanand Saraswati (1824-1883) → Vivekananda (1863-1902).

50-065.r: Prarthana Samaj → founded 1867 in Bombay (Maharashtra) by Atmaram Pandurang, inspired by Keshab Chandra Sen; M.G. Ranade joined in 1869.
50-065.t: Founder is Atmaram Pandurang, not Ranade (a later member).
50-065.c: No answer printed: the founder, Atmaram Pandurang, is not among the main question's options.

50-070.r: Dev Samaj → founded 1887 at Lahore by Pandit Shiv Narayan Agnihotri (Bhagwan Devatma), an ex-Brahmo; teachings in 'Devshastra'.

50-071.r: Satyashodhak Samaj → founded 1873 by Jyotiba Phule (non-Brahmin movement to free Shudras); he wrote 'Gulamgiri'.

50-078.r: Satyashodhak Samaj (Jyotiba Phule, 1873) → main aim: uplift of backward classes, Dalits and lower castes; books 'Gulamgiri', 'Sarvjanik Satyadharm Pustak'.

50-080.r: Satyashodhak Samaj → an anti-caste movement in Maharashtra; Jyotiba Phule its first president, Savitribai head of the women's section.

50-083.r: Radhakant Deb → Bengali leader who backed orthodoxy; founded Dharma Sabha (1830) and opposed abolition of Sati.

50-084.r: Radha Swami Satsang → founded 1861 by Shivdayal Sahab (Swamiji Maharaj); faith in 'Satnaam' and 'Anami'.

50-085.r: Gopal Hari Deshmukh (1823–1892) → 'Lokahitvadi', the pen name for his social-reform articles in the weekly 'Prabhakar'.

50-087.r: Vishnu Parashuram Pandit → led widow remarriage campaign in Maharashtra; founded Widow Remarriage Association (1850).
50-087.t: B.M. Malabari is known for work against child marriage, not this campaign.

50-088.r: Behramji M. Malabari (born 1853, Baroda) → greatest Parsi social reformer of 19th century; his efforts produced the Age of Consent Act, 1891.

50-090.r: Age of Consent Act, 1891 → advocated by Parsi reformer Behramji Malabari (true); Tilak opposed it (statement 2 false).
50-090.t: Tilak opposed, not supported, the Age of Consent Act.

50-091.r: M.G. Ranade → relied on legislation for social reform; founded Indian National Social Conference (1887, with Raghunath Rao), meeting alongside Congress sessions.

50-092.r: Wrong pair: Social Reform Association (Bombay, 1903) → Chandavarkar, Bhandarkar etc., not Shri Ram Bajpai. Correct: Servants of India–Gokhale (1905); Social Service League–N.M. Joshi; Seva Samiti–H.N. Kunzru.

50-093.r: Rajahmundry Social Reform Association (1871) → Kandukuri Veeresalingam, 'father of Telugu Renaissance'; for widow remarriage, against nautch girls.

50-094.r: National Social Conference → formed because Congress wanted its platform only for political affairs, not social reform.

50-095.r: Correct: Brahmo Samaj under Keshab Chandra Sen campaigned for women's education; Vinoba Bhave's Sarvodaya Samaj worked among refugees. Wrong: Arya Samaj in 1835 (actually 1875); Lajpat Rai opposing Vedas.

50-096.r: 1856 → Hindu Widow Remarriage Act (Vidyasagar's campaign). Religious Disabilities Act never passed in India; Sati banned 1829 (Bentinck); Dalhousie's annexation policy 1848.
50-096.c: No answer printed: only (iii) fits, and no code gives (iii) alone.

50-098.r: D.K. Karve (Western India) → women's education and widow welfare; ran a shelter and school for widows; set up India's first women's university (1916).

50-099.r: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar → his campaign got widow remarriage legalised: Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856.

50-100.r: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar → secretary of Hindu Female School, later Bethune Female School (Bethune College).

50-101.r: False: Ram Mohan Roy supported Sati (he opposed it). True: Bentinck made Sati an offence in 1829; widow remarriage Act 1856; Arya Samaj 1875.

50-102.r: Act V of 1843 → made slavery illegal in India under Lord Ellenborough; the Charter of 1833 had asked to end it.

50-103.r: Keshab Chandra Sen → key role in Native Marriage Act (Brahmo Marriage Act), 1872: minimum marriage age 14 for girls, 18 for boys.

50-105.r: Native (Civil) Marriage Act 1872 (K.C. Sen) → girls' minimum age 14; legalised inter-caste marriage, banned polygamy.
50-105.t: Age of Consent Act (1891, Malabari) forbade marriage of girls below 12; don't mix the two.

50-106.r: B.M. Malabari (Parsi, born 1853) → editor of 'Indian Spectator' and 'Voice of India'; chief crusader for the Age of Consent Act 1891.

50-107.r: Sharda Act (Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929; Har Bilas Sharda) → prevents child marriage; minimum age 14 for girls and 18 for boys.

50-109.r: Theosophical Society → founded 1875 in New York by Madame H.P. Blavatsky and Colonel Henry Steel Alcott; came to India 1879; headquarters Adyar 1882.

50-110.r: Annie Besant (joined 1889, came to India 1893) → main reason for Theosophical Society's success in India; headquarters at Adyar, Madras.

50-111.r: Wrong pair: M.G. Ranade–Theosophical Society (Ranade was in Prarthana Samaj). Correct: Ram Mohan Roy–Brahmo Samaj; Dayanand–Arya Samaj; Vivekananda (not Ramakrishna)–Ramakrishna Mission.

50-114.r: Wrong pair: Atmiya Sabha → Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1815), not Debendra Nath Tagore. Correct: Prarthana Samaj–Atmaram Pandurang; Brahmo Samaj of India–Keshav Chandra Sen; Radhaswami Satsang–Tulsi Ram.
